justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd presume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely around $60 for whatever asset this covers. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $60.45 essentially anchors near the current price, acknowledging that short-term price discovery rarely produces dramatic moves in the absence of a specific catalyst. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $60.80, reflecting a weak positive drift assumption consistent with modest momentum or a slight bullish bias in underlying fundamentals. At the one-month horizon, the $61.50 estimate continues that gentle upward trend, implying no major structural shift but allowing for cumulative drift over a longer holding period.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially across horizons, and this reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the $58.80–$62.10 range is relatively tight because intraday and overnight volatility is constrained and mean-reverting forces are strong. By one week, the $57.50–$64.10 range accounts for the possibility of several consecutive adverse or favorable sessions stacking up. At one month, the $54.00–$69.00 range is quite wide, incorporating the possibility of regime changes, macro data surprises, or sentiment shifts that could meaningfully reprice the asset across a multi-week window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic announcements such as unexpected central bank policy shifts, inflation prints, or employment data that dramatically change rate expectations. Geopolitical shocks or sector-specific news, depending on the asset class, could also produce gap moves that would breach even the one-day interval. On the upside, a surprise earnings beat, unexpected M&A activity, or a broader risk-on rally could push prices well above $69 within a month.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals, while probabilistically calibrated, embed assumptions about volatility regimes that may not hold. If realized volatility is higher than the historical baseline I implicitly used, actual outcomes will fall outside these bands more frequently than the stated 90% coverage would suggest. Liquidity conditions, positioning crowding, and correlation breakdowns in stressed markets are all factors that can cause empirical distributions to have fatter tails than my model anticipates.
